tagline: Red rock spires, a San Juan crossing, and the road to Bluff
intro: US 163 runs through the red rock spires of Monument Valley, crosses the San Juan River at Mexican Hat, and continues toward Bluff. Utah’s legislature designated its Utah length the Bluff to Monument Valley Scenic Byway; it also forms part of the Trail of the Ancients National Scenic Byway. Utah’s Canyon Country highlights the desert formations and river crossing and allows two hours for the drive.

The Utah route first received the State Route 47 designation in 1910. In 1970, a rearrangement of Four Corners highways made it part of US 163, which then extended north to Crescent Junction. US 191 took over much of that northern alignment in 1981, and Utah shortened US 163 to Bluff. The road signs and the national designation did not immediately agree: the northern section remained unsigned, and federal approval to end US 163 at US 191 came in 2008.

From the Arizona line, the drive passes the junction for the Monument Valley visitor center and heads northeast to Mexican Hat. There it crosses the San Juan and leaves the Navajo Nation. Beyond Mexican Hat, the route turns east across Comb Ridge toward Bluff. Bluff sits at the meeting of Cottonwood Wash and the San Juan River.
notice: At Mexican Hat, the byway crosses the San Juan River on a historic bridge.

moments.title: Forrest Gump hill
moments.text: A view area near Utah mile marker 13 acquired the nickname Forrest Gump hill from the film location where the title character ends his cross-country run. The film’s wider frame includes Eagle Mesa, Brighams Tomb and Stagecoach. Eagle Mesa is visible from Highway 163 on Navajo Nation land. Its cliffs rise above Organ Rock Shale, which erodes more readily than the sandstone above it. That unequal erosion helped shape the valley’s mesas and buttes. Eagle Mesa rises 1,100 feet above its surroundings; its upper rock layers include the Moenkopi Formation capped by Shinarump Conglomerate.

moments.title: Mexican Hat
moments.text: Mexican Hat takes its name from the sombrero-shaped rock on the northeast edge of town, a formation 60 feet wide and 12 feet high. The settlement stands on the San Juan River at the northern edge of the Navajo Nation. In 2016, the US 163 river crossing received the name Jason R. Workman Memorial Bridge. Workman, a 1997 graduate of nearby San Juan High School, served with SEAL Team Six and was killed in Afghanistan in 2011. Beyond the crossing, Valley of the Gods lies to the north on US 163, with Goosenecks State Park west-northwest of town.

moments.title: Bluff
moments.text: Bluff’s name comes from the bluffs near its town site. Under John Taylor’s direction, Silas S. Smith and Jens Nielson led about 230 Mormons toward southeastern Utah to establish a farming community. They arrived in April 1880 after forging about 200 miles of trail over difficult terrain, including the passage down Hole in the Rock. The town lies where Cottonwood Wash meets the San Juan, on the north margin of the river valley. Its population fell to seventy by 1930, then rose during the uranium prospecting boom of the 1950s before declining again with uranium in the 1970s.
